contents.html: Device cybersecurity capabilities are cybersecurity features or functions that computing devices provide through their own technical means (i.e., device hardware and software). This publication defines an Internet of Things (IoT) device cybersecurity capability core baseline, which is a set of device capabilities generally needed to support common cybersecurity controls that protect an organization’s devices as well as device data, systems, and ecosystems. The purpose of this publication is to provide organizations a starting point to use in identifying the device cybersecurity capabilities for new IoT devices they will manufacture, integrate, or acquire. This publication can be used in conjunction with NISTIR 8259, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Device Manufacturers.
contents.html_ja: デバイスのサイバーセキュリティ能力とは、コンピューティングデバイスが自らの技術的手段（すなわち、デバイスのハードウェアとソフトウェア）によって提供する、サイバーセキュリティの特徴または機能です。この刊行物は、モノのインターネット（IoT）デバイスのサイバーセキュリティ能力のコアベースラインを定義します。これは、組織のデバイスに加え、デバイスのデータ、システム、エコシステムを保護する一般的なサイバーセキュリティ管理策をサポートするために、一般に必要となるデバイス能力の集合です。この刊行物の目的は、組織が、製造、統合、または調達する新しい IoT デバイスに求めるデバイスのサイバーセキュリティ能力を特定する際に使える、出発点を提供することです。この刊行物は、NISTIR 8259, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Device Manufacturers と併せて使用できます。

contents.html: Computing devices that integrate physical and/or sensing capabilities and network interface capabilities are being designed, developed, and deployed at an ever-increasing pace. These devices are fulfilling customer needs in all sectors of the economy. Many of these computing devices are connected to the internet. A novel characteristic of these devices is the combination of connectivity and the ability to sense and/or affect the physical world. As devices become smaller and more complex, with an increasing number of features, the security of those devices also becomes more complex. This publication defines a baseline set of device cybersecurity capabilities that organizations should consider when confronting the challenge of the Internet of Things (IoT).
contents.html_ja: 物理的な機能やセンシング機能、およびネットワークインターフェース機能を統合したコンピューティングデバイスが、かつてない速さで設計、開発、配備されています。これらのデバイスは、経済のあらゆる分野で顧客のニーズを満たしています。これらのコンピューティングデバイスの多くは、インターネットに接続されています。これらのデバイスの新しい特徴は、接続性と、物理世界を感知する、または物理世界に作用する能力の組み合わせです。デバイスが小型化・複雑化し、機能の数が増えるにつれて、それらのデバイスのセキュリティも複雑になります。この刊行物は、組織がモノのインターネット（IoT）という課題に向き合う際に検討すべき、デバイスのサイバーセキュリティ能力のベースラインの集合を定義します。

contents.html: Device cybersecurity capabilities are cybersecurity features or functions that computing devices provide through their own technical means (i.e., device hardware and software). The IoT device cybersecurity capability core baseline (core baseline)1 defined in this publication is a set of device capabilities generally needed to support commonly used cybersecurity controls that protect devices as well as device data, systems, and ecosystems. The concept of a baseline in any context requires careful consideration; security capabilities for IoT devices are no exception.
contents.html_ja: デバイスのサイバーセキュリティ能力とは、コンピューティングデバイスが自らの技術的手段（すなわち、デバイスのハードウェアとソフトウェア）によって提供する、サイバーセキュリティの特徴または機能です。この刊行物で定義する IoT デバイスのサイバーセキュリティ能力のコアベースライン（コアベースライン）1は、デバイスに加え、デバイスのデータ、システム、エコシステムを保護する、一般的に使われているサイバーセキュリティ管理策をサポートするために、一般に必要となるデバイス能力の集合です。どのような文脈でもベースラインという概念には慎重な検討が必要であり、IoT デバイスのセキュリティ能力も例外ではありません。

contents.html: The core baseline has been derived from researching common cybersecurity risk management approaches and commonly used capabilities for addressing cybersecurity risks to IoT devices, which were refined and validated using a collaborative public-private process to incorporate all viewpoints. Multiple requests for comment were issued, and multiple workshops and roundtables were held. NIST is committed to an open and transparent process that facilitates stakeholder feedback and iterative improvement.
contents.html_ja: コアベースラインは、一般的なサイバーセキュリティリスクマネジメントのアプローチと、IoT デバイスに対するサイバーセキュリティリスクに対処するために一般的に使われている能力を調査して導き出され、あらゆる観点を取り入れるために、官民が協力するプロセスを使って洗練され、検証されました。複数回の意見募集が行われ、複数のワークショップと円卓会議が開催されました。NIST は、ステークホルダーのフィードバックと反復的な改善を促す、公開で透明なプロセスに取り組んでいます。

contents.html: These capabilities were developed in the context of NISTIR 8259, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Device Manufacturers [2], which discusses considerations for manufacturers to help guide them in choosing and implementing the device cybersecurity capabilities their IoT devices will provide. NISTIR 8259 also defines terminology and concepts that provide critical context for understanding device cybersecurity capabilities as one part of the entire IoT cybersecurity ecosystem. Thus, though both NISTIR 8259 and this publication have manufacturers as the intended audience, the considerations and capabilities discussed across the two publications can be used by manufacturers, integrators, or consumers. For more information on how these capabilities can be incorporated into a manufacturer’s development processes, see NISTIR 8259. Other organizations can use the core baseline in the context that is available and appropriate to them.

Device Identification: The IoT device can be uniquely identified logically and physically.
  1. A unique logical identifier
  2. A unique physical identifier at an external or internal location on the device authorized entities can access
Note: the physical and logical identifiers may represent the same value, but they do not have to.
  • This capability supports asset management, which in turn supports vulnerability management, access management, data protection, and incident detection.
  • The unique logical identifier can be used to distinguish the device from all others, usually for automated device management and monitoring. This may require that it be immutable to allow for consistent identification using the identifier. The unique logical identifier may also be used for device authentication, but consideration should be made to select an appropriate identifier for the purpose.
  • The unique physical identifier can be used to distinguish the device from all others whenever the unique logical identifier is unavailable, such as during device deployment and decommissioning, or after a device failure.
  • The capability may also need an additional logical identifier that will not necessarily be unique which is used for more specific purposes such as device intent signaling.

  • This capability supports vulnerability management, access management, data protection, and incident detection.
  • An authorized entity may want to alter a device’s configuration for a variety of reasons, including cybersecurity, interoperability, privacy, and usability. Without a device configuration capability, an authorized entity cannot customize a device to meet its needs, integrate the device into the authorized entity's environment, etc.
  • Most cybersecurity capabilities are at least somewhat dependent on the presence of a device configuration capability.
  • Unauthorized entities may want to change a device's configuration for many reasons, such as gaining unauthorized access, causing the device to malfunction, or secretly monitoring the device's environment.
  • The ability to restore a secure configuration for a device is helpful when the current configuration contains errors, has been damaged or corrupted, or is otherwise no longer thought to be trustworthy.

  2. The ability to logically restrict access to each network interface to only authorized entities (e.g., device authentication, user authentication)
  3. Configuration settings for use with the Device Configuration capability including, but not limited to, the ability to enable, disable, and adjust thresholds for any ability the device might have to lock or disable an account or to delay additional authentication attempts after too many failed authentication attempts
  • This capability supports vulnerability management, access management, data protection, and incident detection.
  • Limiting access to interfaces reduces the attack surface of the device, giving attackers fewer opportunities to compromise it. For example, unrestricted network access to an IoT device enables attackers to directly interact with the device, which significantly increases the likelihood of the device being compromised.
  • Access to interfaces may be partially or completely limited based on the device’s state. For example, if a device has not been provisioned with proper network credentials, all access to/from network interfaces would be limited if using a secure on-boarding scheme.

デバイスのサイバーセキュリティ能力共通の要素根拠IoT の参考例
デバイス識別: IoT デバイスを、論理的にも物理的にも一意に識別できます。
  1. 一意の論理識別子
  2. 認可されたエンティティがアクセスできる、デバイスの外部または内部の場所にある一意の物理識別子
注: 物理識別子と論理識別子は同じ値を表してもかまいませんが、同じである必要はありません。
  • この能力は、資産管理をサポートし、資産管理は、脆弱性管理、アクセス管理、データ保護、インシデント検知をサポートします。
  • 一意の論理識別子は、通常は自動化されたデバイス管理と監視のために、そのデバイスを他のすべてのデバイスと区別するために使えます。識別子を使って一貫した識別を可能にするため、不変である必要がある場合があります。一意の論理識別子はデバイス認証にも使えますが、その目的に適した識別子を選ぶよう考慮すべきです。
  • 一意の物理識別子は、デバイスの配備や廃棄の際、あるいはデバイスの故障後など、一意の論理識別子が利用できないときに、そのデバイスを他のすべてのデバイスと区別するために使えます。
  • この能力には、デバイスの意図の通知など、より具体的な目的に使われる、必ずしも一意ではない追加の論理識別子も必要になる場合があります。

デバイス構成: IoT デバイスのソフトウェアの構成を変更でき、そのような変更を行えるのは認可されたエンティティのみです。
  1. デバイスのソフトウェアの構成設定を変更できる能力
  2. 構成の変更を認可されたエンティティのみに制限できる能力
  3. 認可されたエンティティが、認可されたエンティティによって定義された安全な構成にデバイスを復元できる能力
  • この能力は、脆弱性管理、アクセス管理、データ保護、インシデント検知をサポートします。
  • 認可されたエンティティは、サイバーセキュリティ、相互運用性、プライバシー、使いやすさなど、さまざまな理由でデバイスの構成を変更したいと考える場合があります。デバイス構成の能力がなければ、認可されたエンティティは、自らのニーズに合わせてデバイスをカスタマイズしたり、そのデバイスを認可されたエンティティの環境に統合したりすることなどができません。
  • ほとんどのサイバーセキュリティ能力は、少なくともある程度は、デバイス構成の能力があることに依存しています。
  • 認可されていないエンティティは、不正アクセスの獲得、デバイスの誤動作の誘発、デバイスの環境の秘密裏の監視など、多くの理由でデバイスの構成を変更したいと考える場合があります。
  • デバイスの安全な構成を復元できる能力は、現在の構成に誤りがある場合、損傷または破損している場合、あるいはそれ以外の理由で信頼できると考えられなくなった場合に役立ちます。

データ保護: IoT デバイスは、自らが保存し送信するデータを、不正アクセスおよび改変から保護できます。
  1. 標準化された暗号アルゴリズム（たとえば、認証付き暗号化、暗号学的ハッシュ、デジタル署名の検証）を用いる、セキュリティが実証された暗号モジュールを利用して、デバイスが保存・送信するデータの機密性および完全性が侵害されないようにする能力
  2. 認可されたエンティティが、以前に認可されていたかどうかを問わず、すべてのエンティティからデバイス上のすべてのデータにアクセスできない状態にする能力（たとえば、内部ストレージの消去、暗号化されたデータの暗号鍵の破棄による）
  3. デバイス構成の能力とともに使用するための構成設定。これには、鍵長を選択するなど、認可されたエンティティが暗号の使用自体を構成できる機能が含まれますが、これに限りません。
  • この能力は、アクセス管理、データ保護、インシデント検知をサポートします。
  • 認可されたエンティティ（たとえば、顧客、管理者、ユーザー）は、認可されていないエンティティが自らのデータにアクセスして悪用できないように、データの機密性が保護されることを望むことがよくあります。
  • 認可されたエンティティは、データが不注意または意図的に変更されないように、データの完全性が保護されることを望むことがよくあります。変更されると、機器に誤ったコマンドを発行する、悪意ある活動を隠蔽するなど、さまざまな悪影響が生じる可能性があります。

インターフェースへの論理アクセス: IoT デバイスは、そのローカルインターフェースおよびネットワークインターフェース、ならびにそれらのインターフェースが使うプロトコルとサービスへの論理アクセスを、認可されたエンティティのみに制限できます。
  1. デバイスの中核機能に必要のないローカルインターフェースおよびネットワークインターフェースを、論理的または物理的に無効化できる能力
  2. 各ネットワークインターフェースへのアクセスを、認可されたエンティティのみに論理的に制限できる能力（たとえば、デバイス認証、ユーザー認証）
  3. デバイス構成の能力とともに使用するための構成設定。これには、認証の失敗が多すぎた後に、デバイスが持つ可能性のある、アカウントのロックや無効化、あるいは追加の認証試行の遅延を行う能力を、有効化、無効化し、そのしきい値を調整できる能力が含まれますが、これに限りません
  • この能力は、脆弱性管理、アクセス管理、データ保護、インシデント検知をサポートします。
  • インターフェースへのアクセスを制限すると、デバイスの攻撃対象領域が縮小し、攻撃者がデバイスを危殆化させる機会が減ります。たとえば、IoT デバイスへの制限のないネットワークアクセスは、攻撃者がデバイスと直接やり取りすることを可能にし、デバイスが危殆化される可能性を大幅に高めます。
  • インターフェースへのアクセスは、デバイスの状態に基づいて、部分的に、または完全に制限される場合があります。たとえば、デバイスに適切なネットワーク認証情報がプロビジョニングされていない場合、安全なオンボーディング方式を使っていれば、ネットワークインターフェースとの間のすべてのアクセスが制限されます。

  2. 更新をインストールする前に、その更新を検証し認証できる能力
  3. 認可されたエンティティが、更新されたソフトウェアを以前のバージョンにロールバックできる能力
  4. 更新の操作を認可されたエンティティのみに制限できる能力
  5. 更新を有効化または無効化できる能力
  6. デバイス構成の能力とともに使用するための構成設定。これには次のものが含まれますが、これらに限りません。
    1. リモート更新の仕組みを、更新のダウンロードとインストールが自動的に、または手動で開始されるように構成できる能力
    2. 更新が利用可能になったときの通知を有効化または無効化し、誰に、または何に通知するかを指定できる能力
  • この能力は、脆弱性管理をサポートします。
  • 更新によって IoT デバイスから脆弱性を除去でき、攻撃者がデバイスを危殆化させる可能性が低下します。
  • 更新によって IoT デバイスの運用上の問題を修正でき、デバイスの可用性、信頼性、性能、その他の運用面を改善できます。

  • 更新が重要なアプリケーションや他のシステムとの統合に意図せず影響を与えた場合に備えて、ロールバックの能力を望む組織もあれば、誰かが意図的または不注意でソフトウェアを脆弱なバージョンにロールバックするリスクをなくすことを好む組織もあります。

サイバーセキュリティ状態の把握: IoT デバイスは、自らのサイバーセキュリティ状態を報告し、その情報を認可されたエンティティのみがアクセスできるようにできます。
  1. デバイスのサイバーセキュリティ状態を報告できる能力
  2. デバイスが期待どおりに動作する可能性が高い場合と、サイバーセキュリティ状態が低下している可能性がある場合とを区別できる能力
  3. 状態の表示へのアクセスを、認可されたエンティティだけが閲覧できるように制限できる能力
  4. デバイスの状態情報を維持する責任を負うエンティティを除き、いかなるエンティティ（認可されているか否かを問わず）も状態を編集できないようにできる能力
  5. イベント／状態ログサーバーなど、別のデバイス上のサービスが状態情報を利用できるようにできる能力
  • この能力は、脆弱性管理とインシデント検知をサポートします。
  • サイバーセキュリティ状態の把握は、危殆化の調査、不正使用の特定、特定の運用上の問題のトラブルシューティングを可能にするのに役立ちます。
  • デバイスがサイバーセキュリティ状態を他のエンティティに知らせる方法は、文脈に固有のニーズと目標によって異なりますが、デバイスの外部に保存する必要がある場合もある永続的な記録に、イベントに関する情報を取得して記録すること、外部で処理されるよう監視システムに信号を送ること、IoT デバイス自体のインターフェースで警告を出すことなどが含まれる場合があります。

contents.html: Organizations should keep in mind that the capabilities presented in Table 1 are meant as a starting point to help provide the means stakeholders may need to meet common cybersecurity needs and goals. Risk mitigation areas that customers may pursue is one way to consider cybersecurity needs and goals that may need to be supported by an IoT device through device cybersecurity capabilities. For example, Figure 1 shows the risk mitigation areas and challenges defined in NISTIR 8228, Considerations for Managing Internet of Things (IoT) Cybersecurity and Privacy Risks [3] that would be supported, in part, by the capabilities defined in Table 1. NISTIR 8228 cites additional challenges that the core device cybersecurity capabilities do not address because those challenges generally apply to relatively few IoT devices compared to the applicability of the core capabilities.
contents.html_ja: 組織は、表 1 に示す能力が、ステークホルダーが一般的なサイバーセキュリティのニーズと目標を満たすために必要となる手段を提供する助けとなる、出発点として意図されていることを念頭に置くべきです。顧客が追求しうるリスク軽減領域を考慮することは、IoT デバイスがデバイスのサイバーセキュリティ能力を通じてサポートする必要があるサイバーセキュリティのニーズと目標を検討する一つの方法です。たとえば、図 1 は、NISTIR 8228, Considerations for Managing Internet of Things (IoT) Cybersecurity and Privacy Risks [3] で定義されたリスク軽減領域と課題のうち、表 1 で定義された能力によって一部サポートされるものを示しています。NISTIR 8228 は、コアとなるデバイスのサイバーセキュリティ能力が扱わない追加の課題も挙げています。これらの課題は、コア能力の適用範囲と比べると、一般に該当する IoT デバイスが比較的少ないためです。

contents.html: Figure 1 demonstrates that a broad and common set of risk mitigation areas was considered for the core baseline, which should be understood by manufacturers and other readers using the core baseline as a starting point. Though IoT devices providing the basic device cybersecurity capabilities described in the core baseline may help many customers more easily meet their cybersecurity needs and goals while using IoT devices, in reality, customers will likely target different and more specific risk mitigation areas. Therefore, the six capabilities and common elements in Table 1 should not be considered the universal and complete definition of necessary device cybersecurity capabilities for all customers.
contents.html_ja: 図 1 は、コアベースラインについて幅広く一般的なリスク軽減領域が考慮されたことを示しています。これは、コアベースラインを出発点として用いる製造者やその他の読者が理解しておくべきです。コアベースラインに記述された基本的なデバイスのサイバーセキュリティ能力を備える IoT デバイスは、多くの顧客が IoT デバイスを使用する際に、自らのサイバーセキュリティのニーズと目標をより容易に満たす助けとなる場合がありますが、実際には、顧客は異なる、より具体的なリスク軽減領域を対象とする可能性が高いでしょう。したがって、表 1 の 6 つの能力と共通要素を、すべての顧客に必要なデバイスのサイバーセキュリティ能力の普遍的かつ完全な定義と見なすべきではありません。

contents.html_ja: NISTIR 8259 で説明されているように、製造者は、文脈に応じて必要となる正確なデバイスのサイバーセキュリティ能力を特定するため、各 IoT デバイスの想定顧客と想定ユースケースを考慮すべきです。製造者は、顧客に関する知識と調査に基づき、新たな要素または追加要素を用いてデバイスのサイバーセキュリティ能力をさらに定義することができます。これは、ここで論じている領域以外のリスク軽減を支えるデバイスのサイバーセキュリティ能力（たとえば、侵入テストやその他の形態のコンポーネントのテスト／検証、リスクを低減する特定のネットワークアーキテクチャ）を組み込むこと、あるいは、広く適用できるものではないものの、顧客またはユースケースの文脈では極めて重要なリスク軽減やその他のサイバーセキュリティのニーズと目標を支える、IoT デバイス固有の要素をさらに組み込むことを意味する場合があります。製造者はまた、リスク軽減に加えて、デバイスのサイバーセキュリティとその要素に影響しうる他の考慮事項も念頭に置くべきです。例として、顧客とユースケースに基づく使いやすさ、サイバーセキュリティに関する役割と責任、および顧客がそれらの分担方法にどのような期待を持つか、さらに、顧客のニーズと目標には直接反映されない可能性がある社会全体のサイバーセキュリティのニーズと目標（たとえば、ボットネットの開発に対する防御）が挙げられます。
contents.html: As described in NISTIR 8259, manufacturers should consider their IoT device’s expected customers and expected use cases to begin to identify the precise device cybersecurity capabilities needed in context. Manufacturers can further define the device cybersecurity capabilities with new or additional elements based on their knowledge and research of their customers. This may mean incorporating device cybersecurity capabilities to support risk mitigations in other areas than what is discussed here (e.g., penetration or other forms of component testing/validation, specific network architectures to reduce risk) or incorporating more unique elements for an IoT device that support less broadly applicable, but in the context of a customer or use case vitally important risk mitigations and other cybersecurity needs and goals. Manufacturers should also keep in mind other considerations in addition to risk mitigations that may impact device cybersecurity and their elements, such as usability considerations based on the customer and use case, roles and responsibility related to cybersecurity and how customers may expect them to be distributed, and societal cybersecurity needs and goals (e.g., protection against the development of botnets) that may not be directly reflected in the customer’s needs and goals, to name a few.

Authorized EntityAn entity that has implicitly or explicitly been granted approval to interact with a particular IoT device. The device cybersecurity capabilities in the core baseline do not specify how authorization is implemented for distinguishing authorized and unauthorized entities, but can include identity management and authentication to establish the authorization of entities. It is left to the organization to decide how each device will implement authorization. Also, an entity authorized to interact with an IoT device in one way might not be authorized to interact with the same device in another way.
Configuration“The possible conditions, parameters, and specifications with which an information system or system component can be described or arranged [20].” The Device Configuration capability does not define which configuration settings should exist, simply that a mechanism to manage configuration settings exists.
Core BaselineA set of technical device capabilities needed to support common cybersecurity controls that protect the customer’s devices and device data, systems, and ecosystems.
Cybersecurity StateThe condition of a device’s cybersecurity expressed in a way that is meaningful and useful to authorized entities. For example, a very simple device might express its state in terms of whether or not it is operating as expected, while a complex device might perform cybersecurity logging, check its integrity at boot and report the results, and examine and report additional aspects of its cybersecurity state.
Degraded Cybersecurity StateA cybersecurity state that indicates the device’s cybersecurity has been significantly negatively impacted, such as the device being unable to operate as expected, or the integrity of the device’s software being violated.
Device Cybersecurity Capability Core BaselineSee core baseline.
Device IdentifierA context-unique value—a value unique within a specific context—that is associated with a device (for example, a string consisting of a network address). (This definition is derived from [21].)
EntityA person, device, service, network, domain, manufacturer, or other party who might interact with an IoT device.
InterfaceA boundary between the IoT device and entities where interactions take place. (This definition is derived from [22].) There are two types of interfaces: network and local.
Local InterfaceAn interface that can only be accessed physically, such as a port (e.g., USB, audio, video/display, serial, parallel, Thunderbolt) or a removable media drive (e.g., CD/DVD drive, memory card slot).
Logical IdentifierA device identifier that is expressed logically by the device’s software. An example is a media access control (MAC) address assigned to a network interface.
Network InterfaceAn interface that connects the IoT device to a network.
Physical IdentifierA device identifier that is expressed physically by the device (e.g., printed onto a device’s housing, displayed on a device’s screen).
Software“Computer programs and associated data that may be dynamically written or modified during the device’s execution” (e.g., application code, libraries) [1].
UpdateA patch, upgrade, or other modification to code that corrects security and/or functionality problems in software. (This definition is derived from [23].)

Device cybersecurity capabilities are cybersecurity features or functions that computing devices provide through their own technical means (i.e., device hardware and software). This publication defines an Internet of Things (IoT) device cybersecurity capability core baseline, which is a set of device capabilities generally needed to support common cybersecurity controls that protect an organization’s devices as well as device data, systems, and ecosystems. The purpose of this publication is to provide organizations a starting point to use in identifying the device cybersecurity capabilities for new IoT devices they will manufacture, integrate, or acquire. This publication can be used in conjunction with NISTIR 8259, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Device Manufacturers.

1 Introduction

Computing devices that integrate physical and/or sensing capabilities and network interface capabilities are being designed, developed, and deployed at an ever-increasing pace. These devices are fulfilling customer needs in all sectors of the economy. Many of these computing devices are connected to the internet. A novel characteristic of these devices is the combination of connectivity and the ability to sense and/or affect the physical world. As devices become smaller and more complex, with an increasing number of features, the security of those devices also becomes more complex. This publication defines a baseline set of device cybersecurity capabilities that organizations should consider when confronting the challenge of the Internet of Things (IoT).

Device cybersecurity capabilities are cybersecurity features or functions that computing devices provide through their own technical means (i.e., device hardware and software). The IoT device cybersecurity capability core baseline (core baseline)1 defined in this publication is a set of device capabilities generally needed to support commonly used cybersecurity controls that protect devices as well as device data, systems, and ecosystems. The concept of a baseline in any context requires careful consideration; security capabilities for IoT devices are no exception.

The core baseline has been derived from researching common cybersecurity risk management approaches and commonly used capabilities for addressing cybersecurity risks to IoT devices, which were refined and validated using a collaborative public-private process to incorporate all viewpoints. Multiple requests for comment were issued, and multiple workshops and roundtables were held. NIST is committed to an open and transparent process that facilitates stakeholder feedback and iterative improvement.

These capabilities were developed in the context of NISTIR 8259, Foundational Cybersecurity Activities for IoT Device Manufacturers [2], which discusses considerations for manufacturers to help guide them in choosing and implementing the device cybersecurity capabilities their IoT devices will provide. NISTIR 8259 also defines terminology and concepts that provide critical context for understanding device cybersecurity capabilities as one part of the entire IoT cybersecurity ecosystem. Thus, though both NISTIR 8259 and this publication have manufacturers as the intended audience, the considerations and capabilities discussed across the two publications can be used by manufacturers, integrators, or consumers. For more information on how these capabilities can be incorporated into a manufacturer’s development processes, see NISTIR 8259. Other organizations can use the core baseline in the context that is available and appropriate to them.

Regardless of an organization’s role, this baseline is intended to give all organizations a starting point for IoT device cybersecurity risk management, but the implementation of all capabilities is not considered mandatory. The individual capabilities in the baseline may be implemented in full, in part, or not at all. It is left to the implementing organization to understand the unique risk context in which it operates and what is appropriate for its given circumstance. For more information on how to conduct a risk assessment, see NIST Special Publication 800-30, Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments [3].

1 The usage of the term “baseline” in this publication should not be confused with the low-, moderate-, and high-impact system control baselines set forth in NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-53 [1] to help federal agencies meet their obligations under the Federal Information Security Modernization Act (FISMA) and other federal policies. In that context, the low-, moderate-, and high-impact control baselines apply to an information system, which may include multiple components, including devices. In this publication, “baseline” is used in the generic sense to refer to a set of foundational requirements or recommendations, and the core baseline described is meant to apply to individual IoT devices.

Furthermore, this baseline is not the only set of capabilities that exist. This baseline represents a coordinated effort to produce a definition of common capabilities, not an exhaustive list. Therefore, an implementing organization may define capabilities that better suit their organization. Using these additional capabilities to support IoT device cybersecurity risk management is encouraged. For more information on IoT device security and privacy considerations, see NISTIR 8228, Considerations for Managing Internet of Things (IoT) Cybersecurity and Privacy Risks [4].
2 IoT Device Cybersecurity Capability Core Baseline Definition

Table 1 defines the IoT device cybersecurity capability core baseline. The core baseline’s role is as a default for minimally securable devices. However, device cybersecurity capabilities will often need to be added or removed from an IoT device’s design, integration, or acquisition to best address an organization’s common cybersecurity risks. The core baseline does not specify how the device cybersecurity capabilities are to be achieved, so organizations who choose to adopt the core baseline for any of the IoT devices they produce, integrate, or acquire have considerable flexibility in implementing it to effectively address needs.
Each row in Table 1 covers one of the device cybersecurity capabilities in the core baseline:

The first column defines the capability. Note that Figure 1, which is located in Appendix A, indicates how the capability relates to the risk mitigation areas and challenges defined in NISTIR 8228, Considerations for Managing Internet of Things (IoT) Cybersecurity and Privacy Risks [3].

The second column provides a numbered list of common elements of that capability—elements an organization seeking to implement the core baseline often (but not always) would use in order to achieve the capability. (Note: the elements are not intended to be comprehensive, nor are they in any particular order.)
The third column explains the rationale for needing the capability and its common elements to be included in the core baseline.

The last column lists IoT reference examples that indicate existing sources of IoT device cybersecurity guidance specifying a similar or related capability. Because the table only covers the basics of the capabilities, the references can be invaluable for understanding each capability in more detail and learning how to implement each capability in a reasonable manner. original_blocks.html: Organizations should keep in mind that the capabilities presented in Table 1 are meant as a starting point to help provide the means stakeholders may need to meet common cybersecurity needs and goals. Risk mitigation areas that customers may pursue is one way to consider cybersecurity needs and goals that may need to be supported by an IoT device through device cybersecurity capabilities. For example, Figure 1 shows the risk mitigation areas and challenges defined in NISTIR 8228, Considerations for Managing Internet of Things (IoT) Cybersecurity and Privacy Risks [3] that would be supported, in part, by the capabilities defined in Table 1. NISTIR 8228 cites additional challenges that the core device cybersecurity capabilities do not address because those challenges generally apply to relatively few IoT devices compared to the applicability of the core capabilities.

original_blocks.html: Figure 1: NISTIR 8228 Risk Mitigation Areas Supported by Each Core Device Cybersecurity Capability

Figure 1 demonstrates that a broad and common set of risk mitigation areas was considered for the core baseline, which should be understood by manufacturers and other readers using the core baseline as a starting point. Though IoT devices providing the basic device cybersecurity capabilities described in the core baseline may help many customers more easily meet their cybersecurity needs and goals while using IoT devices, in reality, customers will likely target different and more specific risk mitigation areas. Therefore, the six capabilities and common elements in Table 1 should not be considered the universal and complete definition of necessary device cybersecurity capabilities for all customers. As described in NISTIR 8259, manufacturers should consider their IoT device’s expected customers and expected use cases to begin to identify the precise device cybersecurity capabilities needed in context. Manufacturers can further define the device cybersecurity capabilities with new or additional elements based on their knowledge and research of their customers. This may mean incorporating device cybersecurity capabilities to support risk mitigations in other areas than what is discussed here (e.g., penetration or other forms of component testing/validation, specific network architectures to reduce risk) or incorporating more unique elements for an IoT device that support less broadly applicable, but in the context of a customer or use case vitally important risk mitigations and other cybersecurity needs and goals. Manufacturers should also keep in mind other considerations in addition to risk mitigations that may impact device cybersecurity and their elements, such as usability considerations based on the customer and use case, roles and responsibility related to cybersecurity and how customers may expect them to be distributed, and societal cybersecurity needs and goals (e.g., protection against the development of botnets) that may not be directly reflected in the customer’s needs and goals, to name a few.
Appendix B—Glossary
Selected terms used in this document are defined below.
Authorized An entity that has implicitly or explicitly been granted approval to interact Entity

with a particular IoT device. The device cybersecurity capabilities in the core baseline do not specify how authorization is implemented for distinguishing authorized and unauthorized entities, but can include identity management and authentication to establish the authorization of entities. It is left to the organization to decide how each device will implement authorization. Also, an entity authorized to interact with an IoT device in one way might not be authorized to interact with the same device in another way.
Configuration “The possible conditions, parameters, and specifications with which an

information system or system component can be described or arranged [20].” The Device Configuration capability does not define which configuration settings should exist, simply that a mechanism to manage configuration settings exists.
